title: Rates of reaction: effect of concentration
aim: To investigate how the concentration of a reactant affects the rate of reaction, by measuring the volume of gas produced (magnesium and hydrochloric acid) and by measuring a change in colour or turbidity (sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid).
background: The rate of a reaction is how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed. It can be followed by measuring the volume of gas given off over time, the loss of mass as a gas escapes, or the time taken for a solution to change colour or become cloudy (turbidity).

Collision theory says that particles must collide with enough energy (at least the activation energy) to react. Increasing the concentration of a solution means there are more reactant particles in the same volume, so collisions happen more often. The frequency of successful collisions increases, so the rate of reaction increases.

Method 1: magnesium ribbon reacts with hydrochloric acid to give hydrogen gas: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). The gas is collected in a gas syringe or an upturned measuring cylinder full of water, and its volume is recorded every 10 seconds. The mean rate = volume of gas ÷ time.

Method 2: sodium thiosulfate solution reacts with hydrochloric acid to form a pale yellow precipitate of sulfur: Na₂S₂O₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + SO₂(g) + S(s). The flask is placed on a cross drawn on paper and the time for the cross to disappear is measured. Because the same amount of sulfur is needed to hide the cross each time, rate is proportional to 1 ÷ time.
hypothesis: As the concentration of sodium thiosulfate (or hydrochloric acid) increases, the rate of reaction will increase, because there will be more particles in the same volume and so more frequent successful collisions.

variables.independent: Concentration of sodium thiosulfate solution (8, 16, 24, 32 and 40 g/dm³), made by diluting the stock solution with water; in method 1, the concentration of hydrochloric acid.
variables.dependent: Time taken for the cross to disappear (s), used to calculate rate = 1 ÷ time; in method 1, the volume of hydrogen gas produced in a set time (cm³).
control: Total volume of sodium thiosulfate solution plus water (50 cm³)
Volume and concentration of hydrochloric acid (10 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³)
Size and shape of the conical flask (same depth of liquid)
Same cross on the same paper, viewed from the same height by the same person
In method 1: length and mass of magnesium ribbon, and volume of acid

equipment: Hydrochloric acid, 1.0 mol/dm³ (and 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mol/dm³ for method 1)
Piece of white paper with a black cross drawn on it
Magnesium ribbon cut into 3 cm lengths
Gas syringe (or measuring cylinder and trough of water) with bung and delivery tube
method: Method 2 (disappearing cross): draw a bold black cross on a piece of white paper and place a clean conical flask on top of it.
Use a measuring cylinder to put 10 cm³ of sodium thiosulfate solution and 40 cm³ of distilled water into the flask (concentration 8 g/dm³). Swirl to mix.
Use a separate 10 cm³ measuring cylinder to measure 10 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid.
Add the acid to the flask, swirl the flask once, and start the stopwatch at the same moment.
Look down at the cross from directly above the flask. Stop the stopwatch when the cross can no longer be seen, and record the time.
Pour the cloudy mixture into the waste container in a fume cupboard or well-ventilated area, and rinse the flask thoroughly.
Repeat using 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm³ of sodium thiosulfate solution, with 30, 20, 10 and 0 cm³ of water, so the total volume is always 50 cm³.
Repeat the whole experiment twice more, calculate the mean time for each concentration, and calculate rate = 1 ÷ mean time.
Method 1 (gas collection): set up a conical flask with a bung and delivery tube connected to a gas syringe (or an upturned measuring cylinder full of water in a trough).
Add 50 cm³ of 0.5 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid to the flask, add a 3 cm strip of magnesium ribbon, immediately replace the bung and start the stopwatch.
Record the volume of gas collected every 10 seconds until no more gas is produced.
Repeat with 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, keeping the length of magnesium and volume of acid the same. Plot volume of gas against time for each concentration on the same axes.

safety.hazard: Sulfur dioxide gas produced in the thiosulfate reaction
safety.risk: Toxic and irritates the lungs; can trigger an asthma attack.
safety.precaution: Work in a well-ventilated room, do not lean over the flask for long, dispose of mixtures promptly, and asthmatic students should take extra care.

safety.risk: Irritant to eyes and skin; higher concentrations (2.0 mol/dm³) are more hazardous.
safety.precaution: Wear eye protection and wash splashes off skin with water.

safety.hazard: Hydrogen gas produced by magnesium and acid
safety.risk: Flammable; can form an explosive mixture with air.
safety.precaution: Keep naked flames away from the apparatus.

safety.risk: Plunger may be pushed out and fall if too much gas is produced, breaking glass.
safety.precaution: Clamp the syringe securely and use a small enough piece of magnesium that the gas volume stays within the syringe's scale.

results.notes: Concentration = 40 g/dm³ × (volume of thiosulfate ÷ 50 cm³). Rate = 1 ÷ mean time, given to 3 significant figures; for example 1 ÷ 30 = 0.0333 s⁻¹. Plot rate (y-axis) against concentration (x-axis): the points lie close to a straight line through the origin, so rate is directly proportional to concentration. For method 1, plot volume of gas (y-axis) against time (x-axis) for each acid concentration.

analysis: As the concentration of sodium thiosulfate increased from 8 g/dm³ to 40 g/dm³, the mean time for the cross to disappear decreased from 94 s to 18 s, so the rate of reaction increased.

The graph of rate against concentration is a straight line through the origin. This shows the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of sodium thiosulfate: doubling the concentration from 16 to 32 g/dm³ roughly doubled the rate (0.0217 to 0.0435 s⁻¹).

At higher concentrations there are more thiosulfate particles in the same volume, so they collide with hydrogen ions more frequently. There are more successful collisions per second, so the reaction is faster.

In method 1, the graph of volume of hydrogen against time is steeper at the start for more concentrated acid, showing a faster initial rate. The curve levels off when the magnesium is used up. If the acid is in excess, the final volume of gas is the same for every concentration because the same mass of magnesium is used.

Higher tier: the rate at a particular time can be found from the gradient of a tangent to the volume-time curve. The gradient is steepest at the start, when the concentration of acid is highest, and decreases as the acid is used up.

errors.error: Judging when the cross disappears is subjective, and different people see it at different times.
errors.improvement: Use the same person and the same cross for every run, or use a light sensor and data logger to measure the change in light passing through the solution.

errors.error: Reaction time on the stopwatch when starting and stopping timing.
errors.improvement: Start the stopwatch at the moment the acid is added and repeat each concentration three times to calculate a mean.

errors.error: Temperature changes between runs (room temperature varies), which also affects rate.
errors.improvement: Measure the temperature of the solutions before each run, or stand the flask in a water bath at a fixed temperature.

errors.error: In method 1, some hydrogen escapes before the bung is replaced.
errors.improvement: Place the magnesium in a small tube inside the flask, or hang it from the bung, then tip it into the acid after the bung is in place.

errors.error: Measuring cylinders have low resolution, so the concentrations made up are not exact.
errors.improvement: Use burettes or graduated pipettes to measure the volumes of thiosulfate and water.

examTips: Use collision theory: higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so more frequent collisions and more successful collisions per second. Say 'more frequent', not just 'more' collisions.
Rate = 1 ÷ time for the disappearing cross method; mean rate = quantity of product ÷ time for gas collection (for example cm³/s).
Keep the total volume the same when diluting (for example thiosulfate plus water always 50 cm³), otherwise the depth of liquid over the cross changes and the test is not fair.
Higher: to find the rate at a particular time, draw a tangent to the curve and calculate its gradient (change in y ÷ change in x).
Know the alternative to a gas syringe: an upturned measuring cylinder or burette full of water in a trough (collection over water).

questions.question: Why does the cross disappear when sodium thiosulfate reacts with hydrochloric acid?
options: A gas is produced that hides the cross
The solution turns dark blue
A precipitate of sulfur forms and makes the solution cloudy
The flask gets hot and steams up
markScheme: 1 mark: a (pale yellow) precipitate of sulfur forms / the solution becomes cloudy (opaque)
questions.explanation: Insoluble sulfur forms as tiny solid particles, which make the mixture cloudy until the cross can no longer be seen. Sulfur dioxide gas is also produced, but it is colourless.

questions.question:
The mean time for the cross to disappear was 46 s.
Calculate the rate of reaction using rate = 1 ÷ time. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: 1 ÷ 46 = 0.02174, which is 0.0217 s⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.

questions.question:
A student recorded these times for one concentration: 22 s, 24 s and 23 s.
Calculate the mean time.
questions.explanation: Add the three times (69 s) and divide by 3.

questions.question: Use collision theory to explain why increasing the concentration of sodium thiosulfate increases the rate of reaction.
acceptedAnswers: more particles in the same volume
markScheme: 1 mark: more (reactant) particles in the same volume
1 mark: particles collide more frequently / more collisions per second
1 mark: more successful collisions per second (so the rate increases)
questions.explanation: The key idea is frequency. The particles do not gain more energy at higher concentration; they just collide more often.

questions.question: To make sodium thiosulfate solutions of different concentrations, the student adds water so the total volume is always 50 cm³. Why?
options: So that the depth of liquid over the cross is the same each time (a fair test)
So that the reaction produces more sulfur
To make the solution warmer
So that the acid is in excess
markScheme: 1 mark: to keep the total volume / depth of solution the same (fair test, only concentration changes)
questions.explanation: If the volume changed, the depth of cloudy liquid you look through would change, affecting when the cross disappears. Only the concentration should vary.

questions.question:
The stock sodium thiosulfate solution has a concentration of 40 g/dm³. A student mixes 30 cm³ of it with 20 cm³ of water.
Calculate the concentration of sodium thiosulfate in the mixture.
questions.explanation: The thiosulfate has been diluted from 30 cm³ to 50 cm³, so its concentration is 30/50 of the original: 0.6 × 40 = 24 g/dm³.

questions.question:
When magnesium reacted with 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, 36 cm³ of hydrogen was collected in 45 seconds.
Calculate the mean rate of reaction in cm³/s.
markScheme: 1 mark: mean rate = volume ÷ time = 36 ÷ 45
1 mark: 0.80 cm³/s
questions.explanation: Mean rate = quantity of product formed ÷ time taken. Dividing time by volume (45 ÷ 36 = 1.25) gives the wrong units.

questions.question: Which piece of apparatus could be used instead of a gas syringe to measure the volume of hydrogen produced?
options: A burette with its tap open, standing upright in air
An upturned measuring cylinder full of water in a trough of water
A conical flask on a balance
A beaker turned upside down on the bench
markScheme: 1 mark: an upturned measuring cylinder full of water (collection over water)
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bubbles into the measuring cylinder and pushes the water out, so the volume can be read from the scale. A balance measures mass lost, which is very small for hydrogen.

questions.question: Suggest one problem with judging when the cross disappears, and how the method could be improved to deal with it.
markScheme: 1 mark: the end point is subjective / different people see the cross disappear at different times
1 mark: use the same person and same cross each time / use a light sensor and data logger
questions.explanation: A light sensor removes human judgement, which improves the reproducibility of the results.

questions.question: Explain why this practical should be carried out in a well-ventilated room.
markScheme: 1 mark: sulfur dioxide (gas) is produced
1 mark: it is toxic / irritates the lungs / can trigger asthma
questions.explanation: Sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid produce sulfur dioxide as well as sulfur. Ventilation stops the gas building up in the room.

questions.question: The graph of rate against concentration of sodium thiosulfate is a straight line through the origin. What does this show?
options: Rate is inversely proportional to concentration
Rate does not depend on concentration
Rate is directly proportional to concentration
Time is directly proportional to concentration
markScheme: 1 mark: rate is directly proportional to concentration
questions.explanation: A straight line through the origin means that doubling one variable doubles the other. Time, not rate, is inversely proportional to concentration.

questions.question:
A tangent was drawn to the volume of hydrogen against time curve at 20 s. The tangent passes through the points (0 s, 6 cm³) and (40 s, 54 cm³).
Calculate the rate of reaction at 20 s.
markScheme: 1 mark: gradient = (54 − 6) ÷ (40 − 0)
1 mark: 1.2 cm³/s
questions.explanation: The rate at a given time is the gradient of the tangent: change in volume ÷ change in time = 48 ÷ 40 = 1.2 cm³/s.

questions.question:
Magnesium was reacted with excess hydrochloric acid of two different concentrations, using the same length of magnesium ribbon each time.
Explain why the same total volume of hydrogen was collected in both experiments.
markScheme: 1 mark: the same mass / amount of magnesium was used
1 mark: magnesium is the limiting reactant (the acid is in excess), so the amount of product depends only on the magnesium
questions.explanation: Concentration changes how fast the hydrogen is made, not how much. The total amount of product is set by the reactant that runs out first.

questions.question: In the disappearing cross experiment, what is the dependent variable?
options: Concentration of sodium thiosulfate
Volume of hydrochloric acid
Temperature of the solution
Time taken for the cross to disappear
markScheme: 1 mark: time taken for the cross to disappear
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured. Concentration is the independent variable (changed), and the acid volume and temperature are control variables.

questions.question: Describe how a student could investigate the effect of the concentration of sodium thiosulfate solution on the rate of its reaction with hydrochloric acid.
markScheme: Indicative content: draw a cross on paper and place a conical flask on it; measure a volume of sodium thiosulfate solution and water with measuring cylinders (for example 10 cm³ + 40 cm³) so total volume is constant (50 cm³); measure 10 cm³ of hydrochloric acid; add acid, swirl and start stopwatch; look down through the flask from above; stop timing when the cross disappears; repeat with different volumes of thiosulfate and water (20 + 30, 30 + 20 and so on); keep volume and concentration of acid, total volume, temperature and the cross the same; repeat three times and calculate mean; rate = 1 ÷ time; plot rate against concentration; ventilate the room because of sulfur dioxide
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, logically ordered method describing how concentration is varied, how time is measured, control variables, repeats and how rate is calculated.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a workable method with the main steps, but some detail missing, such as how dilutions are made or how rate is calculated.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as mix the chemicals and time how long the cross takes to disappear.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Top answers explain how the concentration is changed (dilution with water at constant total volume), what is timed, and how the results are made valid and repeatable.
